indicativeContent: Data Protection Act 2018 / UK GDPR principles: lawfulness, purpose limitation, data minimisation
Rights of data subjects (access, erasure) and how outsourcing affects them
International transfer rules — adequacy, safeguards, or explicit consent required for overseas processing
Security obligations: encryption in transit/at rest, breach notification within 72 hours
Ethical duties beyond law: patient trust, re-identification risk from pseudonymised data
Accountability: the trust remains data controller even when processing is outsourced
Balanced conclusion weighing clinical/operational benefits against privacy risk

questions.prompt: A logistics company processes delivery routes on datasets that are nearly sorted, with occasional new insertions. Evaluate whether insertion sort, merge sort, or quicksort is the best choice for their routing system, justifying your recommendation.

indicativeContent: Insertion sort is O(n) on nearly-sorted input — adaptive behaviour suits this exact data profile
Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) regardless of input but costs O(n) extra memory
Quicksort averages O(n log n) but degrades to O(n²) on sorted/nearly-sorted data with naive pivot choice
Insertion sort's low overhead and in-place operation suit small-to-medium route lists
For large datasets the quadratic worst case of insertion sort may dominate — dataset size matters
Stability may matter if equal-priority deliveries must keep original ordering
Justified recommendation tied to the scenario's stated characteristics

Abstraction: road network as weighted graph, irrelevant detail (vehicle colour, road names) discarded

questions.prompt: A hospital trust proposes triaging A&E patients using a machine-learning model trained on five years of historical admissions data. Discuss the ethical, legal and technical issues raised by deploying algorithmic decision-making in this context, and evaluate whether the benefits justify the risks.

levels.title: Level 3 (High Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Comprehensive, accurate knowledge of training-data bias, concept drift, accountability, GDPR/DPA 2018 principles and human-in-the-loop design.
levels.ao2: Detailed, sustained application: historical admissions encode demographic bias, model errors have asymmetric costs, clinician override workflows.
levels.ao3: Balanced, nuanced evaluation weighing efficiency and consistency gains against fairness, accountability and automation-bias risks, reaching a substantiated conclusion.

levels.title: Level 2 (Medium Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Some accurate knowledge of training data, bias sources and data protection principles.
levels.ao2: Applies concepts to the triage scenario with mostly clear reasoning.
levels.ao3: Some evaluation present though imbalanced.

levels.title: Level 1 (Low Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Isolated references to bias or privacy with little technical vocabulary.
levels.ao2: Little application to the hospital scenario.
levels.ao3: One-sided assertion.

indicativeContent: Training data reflects historical practice: if past triage disadvantaged groups, the model inherits and amplifies that bias
Correlation vs causation — the model may proxy protected characteristics (postcode, language) even if excluded
GDPR/DPA 2018 Article 22: right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant effect; lawful basis and DPIA required
Accountability: when a triage decision harms a patient, responsibility is diffuse across vendor, trust and clinician
Automation bias: staff may defer to the model even when clinical judgement disagrees
Benefits: consistency, speed, 24/7 uniformity, freeing clinician time — strongest when the model augments rather than replaces judgement
Concept drift: disease patterns and population change, degrading model accuracy without monitoring

questions.prompt: A software house must rebuild a large legacy procedural codebase (a payroll and HR system) and is deciding between an object-oriented and a functional design. Evaluate the suitability of object-oriented programming for large-scale business systems such as this, compared with alternative paradigms.

levels.title: Level 3 (High Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Comprehensive knowledge of OOP principles, composition vs inheritance, functional immutability and modular design tradeoffs.
levels.ao2: Detailed application: payroll rules as polymorphic strategies, employee lifecycle as object state, immutability aiding audit trails.
levels.ao3: Balanced evaluation of maintainability, testability, team scaling and real-world modelling against OOP's verbosity and inheritance fragility, with a substantiated recommendation.

levels.title: Level 2 (Medium Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Sound knowledge of encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and at least one alternative paradigm.
levels.ao2: Applies paradigm features to the business-system context with reasonable clarity.
levels.ao3: Evaluation present but unevenly developed.

levels.title: Level 1 (Low Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Isolated facts about classes or inheritance.
levels.ao2: Generic statements unapplied to payroll/HR.
levels.ao3: One-sided preference without justification.

indicativeContent: OOP strengths: encapsulation protects payroll invariants; polymorphism handles varied employee types cleanly
Domain modelling: business entities (employee, payslip, department) map naturally onto objects with identity and lifecycle
Inheritance pitfalls: fragile base classes, deep hierarchies resisting change — composition often preferable
Functional alternative: immutable data eases audit trails and concurrency; pure functions simplify testing of payroll calculations
Team scaling: encapsulation boundaries let large teams work in parallel with stable interfaces
Testing: OOP statefulness complicates unit tests; functional cores are trivially testable — hybrid designs common
Pragmatic conclusion: most large systems blend paradigms — OO structure with functional cores for calculation-heavy logic

questions.prompt: 'The layered design of network protocol stacks is more important to the success of the internet than any individual protocol.' Discuss this statement with reference to the TCP/IP model, considering how layering affects interoperability, evolution and fault isolation.

levels.title: Level 3 (High Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Comprehensive, accurate knowledge of layer responsibilities, encapsulation, protocol data units and standardisation processes.
levels.ao2: Detailed, coherent application: layer substitution examples (WiFi vs Ethernet, IPv4 vs IPv6), application protocols evolving independently of transport.
levels.ao3: Critical, balanced evaluation weighing the statement against counter-arguments (TCP's centrality, ossification, middlebox interference), reaching a substantiated judgement.

levels.title: Level 2 (Medium Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Sound knowledge of the TCP/IP layers and the role of encapsulation, with some development.
levels.ao2: Applies layering to interoperability or evolution with mostly clear reasoning.
levels.ao3: Evaluation present though incomplete or unbalanced.

levels.title: Level 1 (Low Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Names some protocols or layers without structure.
levels.ao2: Barely linked to the statement.
levels.ao3: Agreement or disagreement asserted without support.

indicativeContent: Layer responsibilities: link (framing, MAC), internet (addressing/routing), transport (end-to-end reliability), application (service semantics)
Interoperability: a browser works identically over Ethernet, WiFi or 5G because only the link layer changes
Independent evolution: HTTP/1.1 → 2 → 3 progressed without rewriting IP; TLS inserted without altering applications
Encapsulation: each layer adds headers, treating the layer above as opaque payload — the mechanism enabling substitution
Fault isolation: layer boundaries localise failures — a cable fault is a link issue, congestion a transport concern
Counter-argument: the end-to-end reliability of TCP and universal addressing of IP are themselves pivotal achievements
Ossification: middleboxes now assume TCP/IPv4, impeding deployment of alternatives — layering succeeded so well it froze
Conclusion: layering is the architectural enabler, but the statement understates the co-evolution of key protocols
